content: Vitamin A, also known as Retinol, is synthesized by the human body from beta-carotene. It plays a protective role against solar radiation damage in dark green, yellow, and orange vegetables and fruits, and is believed to have a similar protective function in the human body. Foods particularly rich in beta-carotene include carrots, squash, broccoli, sweet potatoes, tomatoes (which derive their red color from lycopene), kale, seabuckthorn, collards, cantaloupe, peaches, and apricots. Vitamin C, or Ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble compound that performs multiple essential functions in biological systems. It is abundantly found in citrus fruits such as oranges and sweet lime, as well as in green peppers, broccoli, green leafy vegetables, black currants, strawberries, blueberries, seabuckthorn, raw cabbage, and tomatoes. The late Linus Pauling was a prominent advocate for the use of Vitamin C. Vitamin E, which includes Tocotrienols and Tocopherols, is a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects lipids from oxidative damage. Sources of Vitamin E include wheat germ, seabuckthorn, nuts, seeds, whole grains, green leafy vegetables, vegetable oils, and fish-liver oil. Recent research has demonstrated that certain tocotrienol isomers possess significant antioxidant properties. Coenzyme Q10 is a vitamin cofactor with antioxidant properties. Manganese, particularly in its +2 valence state, functions as a critical component of the enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD), which plays a role in neutralizing reactive oxygen species. Melatonin, a hormone, also exhibits antioxidant activity. Lycopene, a carotenoid terpenoid, is found in high concentrations in ripe red tomatoes. Lutein is abundant in spinach and red peppers. Beta-carotene is present in high amounts in butternut squash, carrots, orange bell peppers, pumpkins, and sweet potatoes. Zeaxanthin is the primary pigment in yellow corn. Astaxanthin, a red pigment, is naturally found in red algae and marine animals higher in the food chain, such as crustaceans and salmon. Canthaxanthin is another carotenoid with antioxidant properties. Flavonoids, a subset of polyphenolic antioxidants, are widely distributed in berries, coffee, and tea. Specific flavonoid subtypes include: Flavones such as luteolin, apigenin, and tangeritin. Flavonols such as quercetin (and its derivatives like rutin), kaempferol, myricetin (abundant in walnuts), and isorhamnetin. Proanthocyanidins, also known as condensed tannins. Flavanones such as hesperetin (a metabolite of hesperidin), naringenin (derived from naringin), and eriodictyol. Flavanols and their polymers, including catechin, gallocatechin, and their gallate esters, as well as epicatechin, epigallocatechin, and their gallate esters. Theaflavins and thearubigins are also included in this group. Isoflavones, which are phytoestrogens primarily found in soy, peanuts, and other members of the Fabaceae family. Examples include genistein, daidzein, and glycitein. Stilbenoids such as resveratrol, which is concentrated in the skins of dark-colored grapes and red wine, and pterostilbene, a methoxylated analogue of resveratrol found in Vaccinium berries. Anthocyanins, which include cyanidin, delphinidin, malvidin, pelargonidin, peonidin, and petunidin. Phenolic acids and their esters include: Ellagic acid, found in high concentrations in raspberries and strawberries, and in ester form in red wine tannins. Gallic acid, present in gallnuts, sumac, witch hazel, tea leaves, oak bark, and other plants. Salicylic acid, found in most vegetables, fruits, and herbs, but most abundantly in willow tree bark, from which it was historically extracted for aspirin production. Rosmarinic acid, abundant in rosemary, oregano, lemon balm, sage, and marjoram. Cinnamic acid and its derivatives, such as ferulic acid, found in seeds of plants like brown rice, whole wheat, oats, and in coffee, apples, artichokes, peanuts, oranges, and pineapples. Chlorogenic acid, a product of caffeic acid esterification, is highly concentrated in coffee (especially robusta beans), blueberries, and tomatoes. Chicoric acid, another derivative of caffeic acid, is found in the medicinal herb Echinacea purpurea. Gallotannins, hydrolyzable tannin polymers formed when gallic acid esterifies and binds with the hydroxyl group of a polyol carbohydrate like glucose. Ellagitannins, hydrolyzable tannin polymers formed when ellagic acid esterifies and binds with the hydroxyl group of a polyol carbohydrate like glucose. Emblicanin, a tannin antioxidant derived from Emblica officinalis (Indian gooseberry). Other nonflavonoid phenolics include curcumin, xanthones, silymarin (a mixture of flavonolignans extracted from milk thistle), and eugenol. Other organic antioxidants include: Citric acid, oxalic acid, and phytic acid. Lignans, which are antioxidants and phytoestrogens found in oats, flax seeds, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, rye, soybeans, broccoli, beans, and some berries. Bilirubin, a breakdown product of hemoglobin, which has been identified as a potentially significant antioxidant. Uric acid, which accounts for approximately half of the antioxidant capacity of human plasma. R-α-Lipoic acid, a compound that is both fatand water-soluble. N-Acetylcysteine, a water-soluble antioxidant.
